newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Europe goes to war against illegal drug barons.
newsitem.headline: Europe goes to war against illegal drug barons.

text.p: Europe has launched a high-profile drive to rid itself of drugs and organised crime, seeking to capture the imagination of citizens increasingly threatened by drug addiction and drug-related crime.
As part of a broader plan to enhance the popular appeal of the European Union, bloc leaders meeting in Dublin agreed on Saturday to work together to crack down on drug producers and dealers.

Recognising the international scale of the drug menace, EU leaders pledged to press other states -- from eastern Europe and central Asia to the Caribbean and Latin America -- to join the war against drug barons who peddle narcotics worldwide.

Outlining plans to co-ordinate member state customs, police and courts to track down drug consignments and hand out tough jail sentences, Irish Prime Minister John Bruton told reporters: "I believe the enhanced efforts we're making in the area of crime...bring the (EU) enterprise closer to the people."
The 15 member states pledged to curb growing domestic production of synthetic drugs, such as Ecstacy.

They will improve the flow of information between forensic laboratories on the chemical profiling of seized drugs, increase joint customs surveillance operations and set up a directory of operational skills and knowledge.
During the summit, EU leaders urged 10 eastern European states who want to join the union to crack down on the growing export of opiates and heroin across their frontiers.
Irish officials said a similar crackdown in the Balkans and former Communist bloc would bolster EU measures.
"Our cooperation...could be focused on developing the kind of law enforcement that will deter drug traffic," one said.

Western drug agencies say east Europe is a key transit route for opiates and heroin grown in the Asian sub-continent and moved through what used to be called the "Silk Road" from Afghanistan to Moscow and western Europe.
The EU will also give the Hague-based Europol, seen as a future European police agency, sharper operational teeth.

"We're very keen to work with Europol. Many of the problems of crime that afflict northern Europe are international," British Prime Minister John Major said. "The advantages of working together are clear."

Ireland, increasingly the final destination for drugs from Europe and beyond -- there are an estimated 10,000 heroin addicts in Dublin alone -- has given the issue a high profile during its six-month EU presidency.
Its anti-drug crusade moved up several gears in the summer when the nation's top investigative reporter was allegedly gunned down by a drug baron's contract killer.

The Netherlands, which takes over the EU presidency next month, has managed to cling on to its famed "coffee-shops" which are central to a 20-year experiment in tolerating the use of small amounts of soft drugs, but will come under continued pressure to fall into line with the rest of Europe.
French President Jacques Chirac, the most vociferous critic of Dutch policy, said on Saturday that "making the Netherlands budge on this is very difficult."
France blames Dutch for attracting thousands of young "tourists" who buy cheap drugs to bring back and sell in France.
But Europe faces a dilemma -- how to crack down on illegal drugs trade while creating a more open Europe, where everyone can travel freely without passports and border controls.
"The public must not think: 'Now the borders are open in Europe, but we have lost our internal security' -- they must think the opposite," said German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
